opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think explainable AI is one of the most important tools we have for auditing these models, and dermatology is a great case study because the stakes are high and the models can look very impressive on paper.

The core problem is that a dermatology classifier can reach high accuracy on a benchmark while relying on the wrong signals. Earlier work showed that some melanoma classifiers picked up on things like surgical skin markings or rulers in the image. Those artifacts happen to correlate with malignancy in the training data because clinicians tend to mark or measure suspicious lesions. Accuracy alone won't reveal that. You need to look inside the model's reasoning.

In our group, we've tried to go beyond standard saliency maps for this. Heatmaps tell you *where* the model is looking, but not *what* about that region matters. Is it color, texture, border irregularity, hair, lighting? So we've used generative approaches to produce counterfactual images. We take a lesion image and minimally change it so the model's prediction flips from, say, benign to malignant. Then we show those pairs to board-certified dermatologists and ask what changed and whether that change is medically meaningful.

That gives you a much richer audit. Some attributes the models rely on line up with clinical knowledge, like darker pigmentation or certain patterns associated with melanoma. Others are clearly spurious. Background skin tone, hair density, or image-acquisition characteristics shouldn't be driving a diagnosis, but in some cases they were. That matters for accuracy, and it matters a great deal for fairness, because reliance on skin tone or photographic conditions could mean the model performs differently across patient populations or across clinics.

The broader point is that explainability turns auditing into a collaboration between the AI and domain experts. The model surfaces hypotheses about what it has learned, and clinicians judge whether those hypotheses make sense. I think that loop is essential before deploying these systems, especially consumer-facing ones that are already widely available and not always rigorously validated.

I'd also say explainability isn't a silver bullet. It should complement prospective validation, testing on diverse external datasets, and careful study design. But without it, you're mostly trusting a number on a test set. With it, you can actually understand why the model works or fails, and that's what you need to build trust and fix problems.

r001.rationale: It describes minimally changing a lesion image until the classifier’s prediction flips from benign to malignant, then reviewing the image pair.

r002.rationale: It says saliency heatmaps show where the model looks but not what matters, motivating methods beyond standard saliency maps.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. I'd say explainability is essential for auditing dermatology models, but with a big caveat about what kind of explainability and what question you're actually asking.

The motivating problem is that these models are very good at finding shortcuts. Our group did a study where we took dermatology classifiers, including ones that had been published and in some cases commercialized, and used them to see what they were really relying on to distinguish melanoma from benign lesions. And the striking finding was that a lot of the signal was coming from things that have nothing to do with the biology of the lesion. Dark corners from the dermoscope. The presence of a ruler or ink markings, because clinicians tend to put rulers next to lesions they're already worried about. Hair, or the absence of hair. Skin tone, which is a serious fairness concern. So the model can get an impressive AUC on a benchmark while learning something that would fail the moment it's deployed in a different clinic with a different camera and different habits.

The challenge was that standard saliency maps don't tell you this very clearly. A heatmap will highlight a blob and the dermatologist will squint at it and say, well, maybe. It's not actionable. So we moved toward what I'd call concept-level or counterfactual explanations. We trained a generative model to produce, for a given image, a version that the classifier thinks looks more malignant and a version it thinks looks more benign, and then we had dermatologists look at pairs and describe what changed. That turns the question from "where is the model looking" into "what attributes is the model using," which is something a clinician can actually evaluate against their own expertise. Some of the attributes they identified were legitimate, like pigmentation patterns and border irregularity. Others were exactly those artifacts.

So in terms of assessment, I think of explainability less as a feature you show the end user and more as an auditing instrument. Its job is to surface the hypotheses about what the model learned, and then you go confirm or refute those with targeted tests, holding out images with rulers, stratifying by skin tone, and so on. Explanations alone are not evidence. They're the generator of good experiments.

The other thing I'd stress is that this needs to happen before deployment and with domain experts in the loop. The methods are only as useful as the people interpreting them. A computer scientist looking at a counterfactual won't recognize that a particular change is clinically meaningless, and a dermatologist won't know to ask about it unless the tool makes it visible. That collaboration is really where the value is.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating paired versions of an image that the classifier judges more malignant and more benign, then having dermatologists examine what changed. This communicates using image changes to probe the classifier’s shift between predictions.

r002.rationale: It says standard saliency maps are not clear or actionable and that explanations alone are not evidence, framing them as prompts for targeted tests. This states that feature attribution alone is insufficient for auditing.

astra-6.text:
I think explainable AI can play an important role in auditing these models, because predictive accuracy alone doesn’t tell us whether a model has learned clinically meaningful patterns. A model might perform well on a test set while relying on something incidental in the images, rather than features of the skin condition itself.

Explanations give us a way to investigate that possibility. We can ask what information is driving the prediction, whether that makes clinical sense, and whether the model behaves differently across patient groups or imaging settings. That can help identify problems that an aggregate performance metric would hide.

But an explanation is not, by itself, evidence that a model is trustworthy. We also need to validate the explanation and test the suspected failure mode—for example, by checking whether changing an irrelevant image feature changes the prediction. So I see explainable AI as a tool for generating and testing auditing questions, alongside clinical expertise and careful evaluation across populations.

r001.rationale: The response suggests changing an irrelevant image feature to test a suspected failure, but does not describe examining image changes that move the prediction across a decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It says an explanation alone is not evidence of trustworthiness and must be validated alongside further testing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think explainable AI can play a very important role, because a model can achieve high accuracy and still be using the wrong information. In dermatology, we want to know whether a prediction is driven by clinically meaningful features of a lesion or by something incidental, like a marking on the skin, an image artifact, or the way the photograph was taken.

Explanations give us a way to investigate those possibilities with clinicians. But an explanation itself is not proof that the model is trustworthy. If it suggests that the model relies on a particular feature, we need to test that hypothesis—for example, by changing or removing that feature and checking what happens to the prediction.

So I see explainability as part of an auditing process: it helps us identify potential shortcuts and failure modes that aggregate accuracy can hide. It needs to be combined with external validation and evaluation across patient populations, including different skin tones, to understand where the model is actually reliable.

r001.rationale: The response proposes changing or removing a feature and checking the prediction, but does not describe examining image changes that move the prediction across a decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It says an explanation is not proof of trustworthiness and that a suggested feature reliance must be tested, clearly stating that feature attribution alone is insufficient.
